title: Estimating Classification Difficulty from Data Complexity: A Practitioner’s Framework
content: Knowing how tractable a classification problem is before committing to training runs matters for resource allocation, expectation setting, and stakeholder communication, yet practitioners facing an imbalanced dataset typically acquire that information only after dozens of experiments have completed. We studied 70 imbalanced binary classification datasets (53 training and 17 stratified external validation sets), computed 11 data complexity metrics spanning geometric, neighborhood, and boundary-region properties, trained 9 classifiers from major algorithm families, and built GradientBoosting meta-regressors that predict mean classifier performance from complexity features alone. The resulting framework returns an algorithm-agnostic difficulty estimate for a new dataset without training any classifier on it. Three findings emerge. Different performance metrics rest on different geometric properties: mean_margin dominates accuracy prediction (Gini importance 0.660) and AUC prediction (0.571), while F1 is governed by overlap_region_count (0.313) and mean_feature_relevance (0.271), a divergence confirmed across two meta-learners and three importance methods. Mean classifier performance is strongly predictable—external R² reached 0.760 for accuracy, 0.761 for F1, and 0.784 for AUC, and all three external Spearman ρ values exceeded 0.77 with p < 0.001—but selecting the best individual algorithm is not, since the median top-2 F1 gap of 0.005 sits at a gap/noise ratio of 0.26 and 86.8% of datasets show F1 gaps below 0.05.
